name: Dinebra
look_here_first: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP — think FINE-BRANCHED ANNUAL: an often slender warm-season annual with NUMEROUS almost straight ascending flowering branches scattered along a main axis, like a narrow brush. Check a mature tiny spikelet with 10–20×: typically 2–4 florets in a ca. 2–4 mm laterally flattened spikelet; short glumes and a tiny pointed glume tip (mucro) require a lens, and do NOT by themselves prove subspecies. Look at the leaf sheath for distinct bulbous/papillose-based spreading hairs and examine the true membranous ligule. The existing source photograph shows only broad panicle/leaf features: it cannot certify floret number, sheath-hair bases, glume mucro or mucronata versus other D. panicea subspecies.

comparison_lesson.title: Dinebra mucronate sprangletop versus green sprangletop and lovegrasses
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: MANY THIN BRANCHES + ANNUAL BASE + TINY USUALLY 2–4-FLORET SPIKELETS suggests Dinebra panicea. Subspecies mucronata needs close botanical determination, not an ordinary photo.
quick_split: GREEN SPRANGLETOP / Disakisperma dubium: generally a larger perennial arising from a lasting base, commonly with fewer longer near-fingerlike branches, and larger 4–12 mm spikelets containing about 4–13 florets. MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP / Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata: slender ANNUAL with many ascending slender branches, generally much smaller ~2–4 mm spikelets with ~2–4 florets and often bulbous-based sheath hairs. Counts can overlap at 4 florets, so a single spikelet count isn't decisive. ERAGROSTIS lovegrasses: many have an airy panicle too but individual spikelets have several fertile florets in overlapping ranks, and the branching/spikelet anatomy differs. Within DINEBRA, the other subspecies of D. panicea can look extremely similar; a photograph labeled merely Dinebra panicea is NOT independently sufficient to certify subsp. mucronata. Old Leptochloa mucronata refers to this taxon in the Kew treatment; Leptochloa filiformis and other older names have been applied differently in historical treatments.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Only D. panicea subsp. mucronata is installed. Never create a duplicate for Leptochloa mucronata, and do not treat a species-level macro as subspecies-certified.

what_to_teach_crew: Start at the fine many-branched inflorescence, not the common name 'sprangletop'.
Find true annual rooting and compare with perennial Disakisperma.
Count FLORETS WITHIN ONE tiny spikelet under 10–20× and measure the spikelet; never use branch count alone.
Examine upper glume mucro, papillose sheath hair bases and inner membrane ligule separately.
Distinguish field-level species complex from unproven subspecies; photograph voucher micros.
Remember Leptochloa mucronata synonym but no duplicate canonical card.
visual_needs: Connected WHOLE ANNUAL: rooted fibrous plant, full brush-like panicle and ruler; document lack of perennial rootstock.
PANICLE BRANCH INSERTION: central axis showing many thin, mostly ascending branches with attached spikelets; overall habit alone is provisional.
SPIKELET MACRO 10–20×: mature 2–4 mm spikelet with a millimeter scale, floret count and glumes clearly separated.
UPPER GLUME MACRO 20×: show any actual minute mucro (tiny hard point) and distinguish it from an awn, with photographed glume tip and scale.
LEAF SHEATH AND LIGULE 10–20×: papillose/bulbous hair bases and true membranous leaf-collar ligule; no arrow until photo visibly resolves the structure.
SUBSPECIES CHECK: authenticated herbarium macro for mucronata versus brachiata at same scale; preserve unresolved determination if only a species-level photograph exists.
MATCHED LOOK-ALIKE: side-by-side measured 2–4-flowered Dinebra spikelet and 4–13-flowered Disakisperma spikelet, each with full rooted plant.
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 1 original Dinebra photo and 2 visible broad markers, two explicitly other-species comparisons. Need full spikelet/glume/mucro and subspecies-certified macros.

items.label: 1 · Mucronate sprangletop — original photographed annual
items.image_role: One already physically stored Dinebra source-labelled photo, prior visible-structure arrows retained, no newly invented closeup.
items.caption: The source-tagged original actual Dinebra field photo shows delicate ascending flowering branches and a narrow blade. The two existing arrows point ONLY at those large visible structures; this photograph does not prove subspecies identity, glume mucro, tiny floret number, true ligule or bulbous leaf-sheath hair bases.
items.why_it_matters: Find the fine-branched annual before inspecting one tiny spikelet. A photographed brush-like seedhead is NOT enough for a subspecies-level determination.
items.creator: abelkinser
items.photo_status: Existing 2 broad arrows and creator/CC BY-NC/source preserved; anatomy micros and independently checked subspecies determination pending.

items.label: 2 · GREEN SPRANGLETOP — clearly different species
items.image_role: Existing physically present CC BY-NC green sprangletop comparison only, not an image of Dinebra.
items.caption: This is GREEN SPRANGLETOP (Disakisperma dubium), NOT Dinebra. Compare its generally few, longer one-sided flowering branches and perennial growth with fine-branched annual Dinebra. The 4–13 florets in one spikelet are a botanical key requiring a macro photograph, not a claim verified from this broad photo.
items.why_it_matters: Two commonly called 'sprangletop' grasses need to be separated using a whole plant plus an actual spikelet.
items.creator: John Connolly
items.photo_status: Existing separate taxon photo reused without modification; per-photo NC license/creator retained, microscopic florets not arrowed.

items.label: 3 · PLAINS LOVEGRASS — different grass comparison
items.image_role: Existing genuine other-genus habit photo for an airy-head confusion check, not Dinebra.
items.caption: This is PLAINS LOVEGRASS (Eragrostis intermedia), NOT Dinebra. Airy panicle branches can deceive from a distance; inspect individual spikelets and count florets rather than relying on a fine-grass silhouette. Spikelet anatomy is not directly resolved in this image.
items.why_it_matters: Prevents overconfident 'sprangletop' naming based only on delicate narrow branches.
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.photo_status: Existing Joey image and specific CC BY-NC original photo records retained; comparison only, no arrows.

study_only_photo_links.look_for: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP: native-at-state-scale slender warm-season ANNUAL with many almost straight, very fine ascending branches arranged along a central flowering axis. Close inspection of the 2–4-flowered tiny spikelet reveals an upper glume with minute MUCRONATE projection, which is NOT visible in the current overall photo. Formerly Leptochloa mucronata; don't duplicate.

rows: Numerous fine branches, tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets usually 2–4 florets; confirm subspecies under microscope
Whole rooted plant and same-scale spikelets
Perennial, frequently fewer longer branches, larger ~4–12 mm and 4–13 florets
Lovegrass often airy panicle and multi-floreted spikelets; photo outline is unreliable alone
Very similar annual brushlike appearance; source photo alone cannot separate confidently
Mature glumes, ligula and floret number
